blocks.text: BC Egg Farms: streets and boundaries

items.t: This is a provincial page, not a neighbourhood: egg production in British Columbia is regulated province-wide under the Natural Products Marketing (BC) Act and the British Columbia Egg Marketing Scheme, 1967.
The regulator's office is in Abbotsford: BC Egg (the BC Egg Marketing Board) is at Unit 250, 32160 South Fraser Way, Abbotsford, per its Small Lot Permit application.

blocks.text: BC Egg Farms: the housing stock

items.t: An egg farm is a quota holding plus barns, not just land: BC Egg classifies producers as Backyard Flock (up to 99 hens, no quota or registration), Small Lot (100–399 hens, registration, no quota) and Registered Producers (400 or more quota hens).
Quota is counted in layers: a BC Farm Industry Review Board (BCFIRB) decision records a national allocation increase distributed as 44,475 layers to licensed producers in good standing.

The farm land under an egg operation is usually Agricultural Land Reserve (ALR = Agricultural Land Reserve) land, so the residence caps in the ALR Use Regulation also apply: 500 square metres (m²) principal, 90 m² additional.

blocks.text: BC Egg Farms: rules that affect buyers

items.t: You cannot legally sell regulated eggs at scale without quota: to become a Registered Producer you must be issued quota from the BC Egg Marketing Board, per BC Egg.
Supply management rests on three pillars named by BCFIRB: production control, price control and import control, with quota management a core Egg Board responsibility.

blocks.text: BC Egg Farms: local details a buyer would not know

items.t: Growth quota has strings: BCFIRB's 2020 decision records that quota holders are not eligible to receive growth quota for 12 months following a transfer of any quota, with a business-unit exception.

Conventional housing has a deadline in the background: BC Egg's 2018 allocation rationale encourages phasing out conventional production well ahead of the July 1, 2036 Code of Practice deadline for pullets and laying hens.

blocks.text: BC Egg Farms: development and new projects

items.t: BC Egg Strategic Plan 2025–2029: Board plan naming 100 per cent quota utilization, housing capacity to meet utilization targets through 2036, and simplifying farm transfers as priorities. Status: plan published for 2025–2029 (as of November 3, 2026).

blocks.text: BC Egg Farms: costs and taxes

items.t: The Small Lot entry cost is fixed by the Board: $250 application fee and $250 annual renewal, per the BC Egg Small Lot Permit application.

The land under an egg farm is Class 9 only if it produces: BC Assessment requires a prescribed amount of qualifying primary agricultural products for sale for Class 9, Farm; farm buildings are Class 1.
Egg farms ship through graders, not farm-gate scale: Small Lot Producers are barred from selling to a Registered Shell Egg Station, which is the grading channel Registered Producers use.

blocks.text: BC Egg Farms: risks and due diligence

items.t: Verify the quota, not just the barns: quota transfers need Egg Board approval, and a private transfer is assessed 5 per cent, so the quota on paper after closing is less than the quota before it.
Verify the producer's standing: BCFIRB's allocation decision distributes new quota pro rata only to licensed producers in good standing with the Egg Board.
Verify the land separately: ALR status, municipal zoning and water licensing each sit outside the quota system and must be checked on the parcel itself.

faq.q: Does the barn housing system change what a layer farm is worth?
faq.a: Verify the specific operation's system and standards position with the board and an inspector rather than from listing text.

faq.q: What should I check before buying a farm in BC?
faq.a: Check the ALR status, water source and licences, drainage and flood history, the buildings and any quota or production licences that do or do not transfer with the land. Poultry and egg production in BC are supply-managed, so a sale of the farm does not automatically include quota.

faq.q: What is the ALR and does it apply to farms in BC?
faq.a: The Agricultural Land Reserve is farmland protected by the provincial Agricultural Land Commission. Farm use is generally allowed on ALR land, but subdividing, adding homes or using the land for non-farm purposes usually needs approval, so check a property's ALR status before you offer.
